newsitem.title: USA: US 30-yr T-bond sale better than expected-analysts.
newsitem.headline: US 30-yr T-bond sale better than expected-analysts.

text.p: In the end, the Treasury's $10.0 billion 30-year bond auction, the third and last part of the Treasury's $38.5 billion refunding effort, drew rave reviews on Thursday after previews had indicated it was destined for mediocrity.

"It looks like a terrific result versus expectations for poor results," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc, a primary dealer. "A few people were caught short here, evidently."
The Treasury sold $10.0 billionin 30-year bonds at an average yield of 6.618 percent. Talk going into the sale was for an average yield of 6.63 percent.
"It came in better than expected," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.

Rupkey said the bid-to-cover ratio (the value of bids received over those accepted) of 2.68 was "extremely high" for a 30-year bond auction. Bid-to-cover ratios tend to be erratic in the 30-year bond auctions, Rupkey said, but they are usually "somewhere around 2.3."
Youngdahl said that on a short-term basis the market had been oversold "after a bad performance Wednesday afternoon and quite a bit of volatility overnight."
As a result, the market offered lower prices this morning.

"What happened last night with the dollar-yen getting whacked by comments from (Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke) Sakakibara," said Rupkey. "That pushed bonds down to where dealers thought they could sell them."
The bond market was sharply lower going into the 1300 EST/1800 GMT bidding deadline for the 30-year bond auction.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond was down 22/32. But when the bidding deadline passed, Treasuries began to trim their losses.
When the results of the auction were announced, Treasuries erased the rest of the day's losses and climbed farther into the plus column.
Shortly before 1500 EST/2100 GMT, the 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond was up 21/32 to 102-12/32, yielding 6.57 percent.

"It was fantastic," said Rupkey of the auction. "This is a classic auction where dealers step up to buy at lower prices. This is exactly what they want -- for yields to back up above the prior few sessions and they step in and buy for a flip."
Analysts said participants' basic confidence in the market's fundamental outlook also aided the auction.
They said trading should be fairly quiet on Friday ahead of a three-day holiday weekend.
